The test flags impurity only when impurity is at least 10% of the tested sample. Every question here reduces to one move: decide how much of each bottle to pour into the sample, so that a 'detected' or 'not detected' result splits the possibilities cleanly.

Work in percentages of the sample, not millilitres. If a bottle contributes a fraction of the sample, its impurity percentage is scaled down by that fraction. With two pure bottles contributing nothing, an impure bottle needs to be at least 10% of the whole mixture's impurity.

Results: one sample of equal parts from several bottles can tell 'all pure' from 'something impure'; a bottle with 20% impurity mixed 1:1 with a pure one shows exactly 10% and is just caught; and a 15% bottle is caught in a mixture only if it makes up enough of the sample.
2021-3-25:
We need the least impurity bottle B can hold, given that a 1:1 mixture with a pure bottle tested positive.

The mixture is 10 ml, and only B's 5 ml can carry impurity. For the test to fire, impurity must be at least 10% of 10 ml = 1 ml.

So 5 ml of B holds at least 1 ml of I, i.e. at least 20% of B. Scaled to the whole 50 ml bottle, that is at least 10 ml.

So the answer is D (10 ml or more).
2021-3-26:
Each bottle is wholly P or wholly I, so any impure bottle contributes 100% impurity in its share.

Pour equal amounts from all four bottles and test once. If even one bottle is I, the mixture has at least 25% impurity, which is well above 10%, so it is detected. If nothing is detected, all four are pure.

One test cannot be beaten, and zero tests tell us nothing. So the answer is 1.
2021-3-27:
One bottle has 20% impurity; the other three are pure. We need to find which one.

A single test gives only yes or no, which cannot separate four possibilities, so at least 2 tests are needed.

Two tests suffice. Test 1: mix equal amounts of bottles 1 and 2. If the impure bottle is among them, the mixture has 10% impurity and is detected; otherwise it is clean. Test 2: test one bottle of the pair that tested positive (or one of the other pair if the first test was clean) on its own. A 20% bottle alone is detected, so the result identifies the bottle.

So the answer is 2.
2021-3-28:
Either one or two bottles are pure; the rest have 15% impurity. We only need to tell which of the two cases holds.

Mix equal amounts from all four bottles. The impurity is the average of the four percentages.

If one bottle is pure: (0 + 15 + 15 + 15)/4 = 11.25%, which is at least 10%, so detected.

If two are pure: (0 + 0 + 15 + 15)/4 = 7.5%, which is below 10%, so not detected.

The single test separates the cases, so the answer is D (1).
